A quota will only measure usage for a resource if it matches\\nthe intersection of enumerated scopes.\\n\\nWhen a scope is added to the quota, it limits the number of resources it supports to those that pertain to the scope.\\nResources specified on the quota outside of the allowed set results in a validation error.\\n\\nKubernetes {{< skew currentVersion >}} supports the following scopes:\\n\\n| Scope | Description |\\n| ----- | ----------- |\\n| [`BestEffort`](#quota-scope-best-effort) | Match pods that have best effort quality of service. |\\n| [`CrossNamespacePodAffinity`](#cross-namespace-pod-affinity-scope) | Match pods that have cross-namespace pod [(anti)affinity terms](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node). |\\n| [`NotBestEffort`](#quota-scope-non-best-effort) | Match pods that do not have best effort quality of service. |\\n| [`NotTerminating`](#quota-scope-non-terminating) | Match pods where `.spec.activeDeadlineSeconds`]() is `nil`]() |\\n| [`PriorityClass`](#resource-quota-per-priorityclass) | Match pods that references the specified [priority class](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption). |\\n| [`Terminating`](#quota-scope-terminating) | Match pods where `.spec.activeDeadlineSeconds`]() >= `0`]() |\\n| [`VolumeAttributesClass`](#quota-scope-volume-attributes-class) | Match PersistentVolumeClaims that reference the specified [volume attributes class](/docs/concepts/storage/volume-attributes-classes). |\\n\\nResourceQuotas with a scope set can also have a optional `scopeSelector` field. You define one or more _match expressions_\\nthat specify an `operators` and, if relevant, a set of `values` to match. For example:\\n\\n```yaml\\n  scopeSelector:\\n    matchExpressions:\\n      - scopeName: BestEffort # Match pods that have best effort quality of service\\n        operator: Exists # optional; \\\"Exists\\\" is implied for BestEffort scope\\n```\\n\\nThe `scopeSelector` supports the following values in the `operator` field:\\n\\n* `In`\\n* `NotIn`\\n* `Exists`\\n* `DoesNotExist`\\n\\nIf the `operator` is `In` or `NotIn`, the `values` field must have at least\\none value. For example:\\n\\n```yaml\\n  scopeSelector:\\n    matchExpressions:\\n      - scopeName: PriorityClass\\n        operator: In\\n        values:\\n          - middle\\n```\\n\\nIf the `operator` is `Exists` or `DoesNotExist`, the `values` field must *NOT* be\\nspecified.\\n\\n### Best effort Pods scope {#quota-scope-best-effort}\\n\\nThis scope only tracks quota consumed by Pods.\\nIt only matches pods that have the [best effort](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#besteffort)\\n[QoS class](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/).\\n\\nThe `operator` for a `scopeSelector` must be `Exists`.\\n\\n### Not-best-effort Pods scope {#quota-scope-non-best-effort}\\n\\nThis scope only tracks quota consumed by Pods.\\nIt only matches pods that have the [Guaranteed](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#guaranteed)\\nor [Burstable](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/#burstable)\\n[QoS class](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-qos/).\\n\\nThe `operator` for a `scopeSelector` must be `Exists`.\\n\\n### Non-terminating Pods scope {#quota-scope-non-terminating}\\n\\nThis scope only tracks quota consumed by Pods that are not terminating. The `operator` for a `scopeSelector`\\nmust be `Exists`.\\n\\nA Pod is not terminating if the `.spec.activeDeadlineSeconds` field is unset.\\n\\nYou can use a ResourceQuota with this scope to manage the following resources:\\n\\n* `count.pods`\\n* `pods`\\n* `cpu`\\n* `memory`\\n* `requests.cpu`\\n* `requests.memory`\\n* `limits.cpu`\\n* `limits.memory`\\n\\n### Terminating Pods scope {#quota-scope-terminating}\\n\\nThis scope only tracks quota consumed by Pods that are terminating. The `operator` for a `scopeSelector`\\nmust be `Exists`.\\n\\nA Pod is considered as _terminating_ if the `.spec.activeDeadlineSeconds` field is set to any number.\\n\\nYou can use a ResourceQuota with this scope to manage the following resources:\\n\\n* `count.pods`\\n* `pods`\\n* `cpu`\\n* `memory`\\n* `requests.cpu`\\n* `requests.memory`\\n* `limits.cpu`\\n* `limits.memory`\\n\\n### Cross-namespace pod affinity scope\\n \\n{{< feature-state for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.24\\\" state=\\\"stable\\\" >}}\\n\\nYou can use `CrossNamespacePodAffinity` [quota scope](#quota-scopes) to limit which namespaces are allowed to\\nhave pods with affinity terms that cross namespaces. Specifically, it controls which pods are allowed\\nto set `namespaces` or `namespaceSelector` fields in pod [(anti)affinity terms](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node).\\n\\nPreventing users from using cross-namespace affinity terms might be desired since a pod\\nwith anti-affinity constraints can block pods from all other namespaces\\nfrom getting scheduled in a failure domain.\\n\\nUsing this scope, you (as a cluster administrator) can prevent certain namespaces - such as `foo-ns` in the example below -\\nfrom having pods that use cross-namespace pod affinity. You configure this creating a ResourceQuota object in\\nthat namespace with `CrossNamespacePodAffinity` scope and hard limit of 0:\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: ResourceQuota\\nmetadata:\\n  name: disable-cross-namespace-affinity\\n  namespace: foo-ns\\nspec:\\n  hard:\\n    pods: \\\"0\\\"\\n  scopeSelector:\\n    matchExpressions:\\n    - For example:\\n-->\\n在配置多个[调度方案](/zh-cn/docs/reference/scheduling/config/#multiple-profiles)时，\\n你可以将某个方案与节点亲和性关联起来，如果某个调度方案仅适用于某组特殊的节点时，\\n这样做是很有用的。\\n要实现这点，可以在[调度器配置](/zh-cn/docs/reference/scheduling/config/)中为\\n[`NodeAffinity` 插件](/zh-cn/docs/reference/scheduling/config/#scheduling-plugins)的\\n`args` 字段添加 `addedAffinity`。例如：\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1beta3\\nkind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration\\n\\nprofiles:\\n  - schedulerName: default-scheduler\\n  - schedulerName: foo-scheduler\\n    pluginConfig:\\n      - name: NodeAffinity\\n        args:\\n          addedAffinity:\\n            requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:\\n              nodeSelectorTerms:\\n              - matchExpressions:\\n                - key: scheduler-profile\\n                  operator: In\\n                  values:\\n                  - foo\\n```\\n\\n<!--\\nThe `addedAffinity` is applied to all Pods that set `.spec.schedulerName` to `foo-scheduler`, in addition to the\\nNodeAffinity specified in the PodSpec.\\nThat is, in order to match the Pod, nodes need to satisfy `addedAffinity` and\\nthe Pod's `.spec.NodeAffinity`.\\n-->\\n这里的 `addedAffinity` 除遵从 Pod 规约中设置的节点亲和性之外，\\n还适用于将 `.spec.schedulerName` 设置为 `foo-scheduler`。\\n换言之，为了匹配 Pod，节点需要满足 `addedAffinity` 和 Pod 的 `.spec.NodeAffinity`。\\n\\n<!--\\nSince the `addedAffinity` is not visible to end users, its behavior might be\\nunexpected to them. Use node labels that have a clear correlation to the\\nscheduler profile name.\\n-->\\n由于 `addedAffinity` 对最终用户不可见，其行为可能对用户而言是出乎意料的。\\n应该使用与调度方案名称有明确关联的节点标签。\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\n<!--\\nThe DaemonSet controller, which [creates Pods for DaemonSets](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/daemonset/#how-daemon-pods-are-scheduled),\\ndoes not support scheduling profiles. When the DaemonSet controller creates\\nPods, the default Kubernetes scheduler places those Pods and honors any\\n`nodeAffinity` rules in the DaemonSet controller.\\n-->\\nDaemonSet 控制器[为 DaemonSet 创建 Pod](/zh-cn/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/daemonset/#how-daemon-pods-are-scheduled)，\\n但该控制器不理会调度方案。\\nDaemonSet 控制器创建 Pod 时，默认的 Kubernetes 调度器负责放置 Pod，\\n并遵从 DaemonSet 控制器中设置的 `nodeAffinity` 规则。\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\n<!--\\n### Inter-pod affinity and anti-affinity\\n\\nInter-pod affinity and anti-affinity allow you to constrain which nodes your\\nPods can be scheduled on based on the labels of **Pods** already running on that\\nnode, instead of the node labels.\\n-->\\n### Pod 间亲和性与反亲和性  {#inter-pod-affinity-and-anti-affinity}\\n\\nPod 间亲和性与反亲和性使你可以基于已经在节点上运行的 **Pod** 的标签来约束\\nPod 可以调度到的节点，而不是基于节点上的标签。\\n\\n<!--\\nInter-pod affinity and anti-affinity rules take the form \\\"this\\nPod should (or, in the case of anti-affinity, should not) run in an X if that X\\nis already running one or more Pods that meet rule Y\\\", where X is a topology\\ndomain like node, rack, cloud provider zone or region, or similar and Y is the\\nrule Kubernetes tries to satisfy.\\n-->\\nPod 间亲和性与反亲和性的规则格式为“如果 X 上已经运行了一个或多个满足规则 Y 的 Pod，\\n则这个 Pod 应该（或者在反亲和性的情况下不应该）运行在 X 上”。\\n这里的 X 可以是节点、机架、云提供商可用区或地理区域或类似的拓扑域，\\nY 则是 Kubernetes 尝试满足的规则。\\n\\n<!--\\nYou express these rules (Y) as [label selectors](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors)\\nwith an optional associated list of namespaces. Pods are namespaced objects in\\nKubernetes, so Pod labels also implicitly have namespaces. Any label selectors\\nfor Pod labels should specify the namespaces in which Kubernetes should look for those\\nlabels.\\n-->\\n你通过[标签选择算符](/zh-cn/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors)\\n的形式来表达规则（Y），并可根据需要指定选关联的名字空间列表。\\nPod 在 Kubernetes 中是名字空间作用域的对象，因此 Pod 的标签也隐式地具有名字空间属性。\\n针对 Pod 标签的所有标签选择算符都要指定名字空间，Kubernetes\\n会在指定的名字空间内寻找标签。\\n\\n<!--\\nYou express the topology domain (X) using a `topologyKey`, which is the key for\\nthe node label that the system uses to denote the domain. For examples, see\\n[Well-Known Labels, Annotations and Taints](/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/).\\n-->\\n你会通过 `topologyKey` 来表达拓扑域（X）的概念，其取值是系统用来标示域的节点标签键。\\n相关示例可参见[常用标签、注解和污点](/zh-cn/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/)。\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\n<!--\\nInter-pod affinity and anti-affinity require substantial amounts of\\nprocessing which can slow down scheduling in large clusters significantly. We do\\nnot recommend using them in clusters larger than several hundred nodes.\\n-->\\nPod 间亲和性和反亲和性都需要相当的计算量，因此会在大规模集群中显著降低调度速度。\\n我们不建议在包含数百个节点的集群中使用这类设置。\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\n<!--\\nPod anti-affinity requires nodes to be consistently labeled, in other words,\\nevery node in the cluster must have an appropriate label matching `topologyKey`.\\nIf some or all nodes are missing the specified `topologyKey` label, it can lead\\nto unintended behavior.\\n-->\\nPod 反亲和性需要节点上存在一致性的标签。换言之，\\n集群中每个节点都必须拥有与 `topologyKey` 匹配的标签。\\n如果某些或者所有节点上不存在所指定的 `topologyKey` 标签，调度行为可能与预期的不同。\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\n<!--\\n#### Types of inter-pod affinity and anti-affinity\\n\\nSimilar to [node affinity](#node-affinity) are two types of Pod affinity and\\nanti-affinity as follows:\\n-->\\n#### Pod 间亲和性与反亲和性的类型\\n\\n与[节点亲和性](#node-affinity)类似，Pod 的亲和性与反亲和性也有两种类型：\\n\\n- `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`\\n- `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution`\\n\\n<!--\\nFor example, you could use\\n`requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` affinity to tell the scheduler to\\nco-locate Pods of two services in the same cloud provider zone because they\\ncommunicate with each other a lot. This is determined by\\nverifying that no other pod in the cluster matches the namespace and selector of this pod,\\nthat the pod matches its own terms, and the chosen node matches all requested topologies.\\nThis ensures that there will not be a deadlock even if all the pods have inter-pod affinity\\nspecified.\\n-->\\n#### 调度一组具有 Pod 间亲和性的 Pod   {#scheduling-a-group-of-pods-with-inter-pod-affinity-to-themselves}\\n\\n如果当前正被调度的 Pod 在具有自我亲和性的 Pod 序列中排在第一个，\\n那么只要它满足其他所有的亲和性规则，它就可以被成功调度。\\n这是通过以下方式确定的：确保集群中没有其他 Pod 与此 Pod 的名字空间和标签选择算符匹配；\\n该 Pod 满足其自身定义的条件，并且选定的节点满足所指定的所有拓扑要求。\\n这确保即使所有的 Pod 都配置了 Pod 间亲和性，也不会出现调度死锁的情况。\\n\\n<!--\\n#### Pod affinity example {#an-example-of-a-pod-that-uses-pod-affinity}\\n\\nConsider the following Pod spec:\\n-->\\n#### Pod 亲和性示例   {#an-example-of-a-pod-that-uses-pod-affinity}\\n\\n考虑下面的 Pod 规约：\\n\\n{{% code_sample file=\\\"pods/pod-with-pod-affinity.yaml\\\" %}}\\n\\n<!--\\nThis example defines one Pod affinity rule and one Pod anti-affinity rule. If you put the same file\\nin the search paths list below, kubelet uses it as the credential provider when pulling images.\\n\\n* `{--root-dir:-/var/lib/kubelet}/config.json`\\n* `{cwd of kubelet}/config.json`\\n* `${HOME}/.docker/config.json`\\n* `/.docker/config.json`\\n* `{--root-dir:-/var/lib/kubelet}/.dockercfg`\\n* `{cwd of kubelet}/.dockercfg`\\n* `${HOME}/.dockercfg`\\n* `/.dockercfg`\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nYou may have to set `HOME=/root` explicitly in the environment of the kubelet process.\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\nHere are the recommended steps to configuring your nodes to use a private registry.  In this\\nexample, run these on your desktop/laptop:\\n\\n   1. Run `docker login [server]` for each set of credentials you want to use.  This updates `$HOME/.docker/config.json` on your PC.\\n   1. View `$HOME/.docker/config.json` in an editor to ensure it contains just the credentials you want to use.\\n   1. Get a list of your nodes; for example:\\n      - if you want the names: `nodes=$( kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range.items[*].metadata}{.name} {end}' )`\\n      - if you want to get the IP addresses: `nodes=$( kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type==\\\"ExternalIP\\\")]}{.address} {end}' )`\\n   1. Copy your local `.docker/config.json` to one of the search paths list above.\\n      - for example, to test this out: `for n in $nodes; do scp ~/.docker/config.json root@\\\"$n\\\":/var/lib/kubelet/config.json; done`\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nFor production clusers, use a configuration management tool so that you can apply this\\nsetting to all the nodes where you need it.\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\nVerify by creating a Pod that uses a private image; for example:\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl apply -f - <<EOF\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: Pod\\nmetadata:\\n  name: private-image-test-1\\nspec:\\n  containers:\\n    - name: uses-private-image\\n      image: $PRIVATE_IMAGE_NAME\\n      imagePullPolicy: Always\\n      command: [ \\\"echo\\\", \\\"SUCCESS\\\" ]\\nEOF\\n```\\n```\\npod/private-image-test-1 created\\n```\\n\\nIf everything is working, then, after a few moments, you can run:\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl logs private-image-test-1\\n```\\nand see that the command outputs:\\n```\\nSUCCESS\\n```\\n\\nIf you suspect that the command failed, you can run:\\n```shell\\nkubectl describe pods/private-image-test-1 | grep 'Failed'\\n```\\nIn case of failure, the output is similar to:\\n```\\n  Fri, 26 Jun 2015 15:36:13 -0700    Fri, 26 Jun 2015 15:39:13 -0700    19    {kubelet node-i2hq}    spec.containers{uses-private-image}    failed        Failed to pull image \\\"user/privaterepo:v1\\\": Error: image user/privaterepo:v1 not found\\n```\\n\\n\\nYou must ensure all nodes in the cluster have the same `.docker/config.json`.  Otherwise, pods will run on\\nsome nodes and fail to run on others.  For example, if you use node autoscaling, then each instance\\ntemplate needs to include the `.docker/config.json` or mount a drive that contains it.\\n\\nAll pods will have read access to images in any private registry once private\\nregistry keys are added to the `.docker/config.json`.\\n\\n### Pre-pulled Images\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nThis approach is suitable if you can control node configuration.  It\\nwill not work reliably if your cloud provider manages nodes and replaces\\nthem automatically.\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\nBy default, the kubelet tries to pull each image from the specified registry.\\nHowever, if the `imagePullPolicy` property of the container is set to `IfNotPresent` or `Never`,\\nthen a local image is used (preferentially or exclusively, respectively).\\n\\nIf you want to rely on pre-pulled images as a substitute for registry authentication,\\nyou must ensure all nodes in the cluster have the same pre-pulled images.\\n\\nThis can be used to preload certain images for speed or as an alternative to authenticating to a private registry.\\n\\nAll pods will have read access to any pre-pulled images.\\n\\n### Specifying ImagePullSecrets on a Pod\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nThis is the recommended approach to run containers based on images\\nin private registries.\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\nKubernetes supports specifying container image registry keys on a Pod.\\n\\n#### Creating a Secret with a Docker Config\\n\\nRun the following command, substituting the appropriate uppercase values:\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl create secret docker-registry <name> `GET`のリクエストを送信します。\\n  レスポンスのステータスコードが200以上400未満の際に診断を成功とみなします。\\n\\n`tcpSocket`\\n: PodのIPアドレスに対して、指定されたポートでTCPチェックを行います。\\n  そのポートが空いていれば診断を成功とみなします。\\n  オープンしてすぐにリモートシステム(コンテナ)が接続を切断した場合、健全な状態としてカウントします。\\n\\n### Probeの結果 {#probe-outcome}\\n\\n各Probe 次の3つのうちの一つの結果を持ちます:\\n\\n`Success`\\n: コンテナの診断が成功しました。\\n\\n`Failure`\\n: コンテナの診断が失敗しました。\\n\\n`Unknown`\\n: コンテナの診断自体が失敗しました(何も実行する必要はなく、kubeletはさらにチェックを行います)。\\n\\n### Probeの種類 {#types-of-probe}\\n\\nkubeletは3種類のProbeを実行中のコンテナで行い、また反応することができます:\\n\\n`livenessProbe`\\n: コンテナが動いているかを示します。\\n  livenessProbeに失敗すると、kubeletはコンテナを殺します、そしてコンテナは[restart policy](#restart-policy)に従います。\\n  コンテナにlivenessProbeが設定されていない場合、デフォルトの状態は`Success`です。\\n\\n`readinessProbe`\\n: コンテナがリクエスト応答する準備ができているかを示します。\\n  readinessProbeに失敗すると、エンドポイントコントローラーにより、ServiceからそのPodのIPアドレスが削除されます。\\n  initial delay前のデフォルトのreadinessProbeの初期値は`Failure`です。\\n  コンテナにreadinessProbeが設定されていない場合、デフォルトの状態は`Success`です。\\n\\n`startupProbe`\\n: コンテナ内のアプリケーションが起動したかどうかを示します。\\n  startupProbeが設定された場合、完了するまでその他のすべてのProbeは無効になります。\\n  startupProbeに失敗すると、kubeletはコンテナを殺します、そしてコンテナは[restart policy](#restart-policy)に従います。\\n  コンテナにstartupProbeが設定されていない場合、デフォルトの状態は`Success`です。\\n\\nlivenessProbe、readinessProbeまたはstartupProbeを設定する方法の詳細については、[Liveness Probe、Readiness ProbeおよびStartup Probeを使用する](/ja/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)を参照してください。\\n\\n#### livenessProbeをいつ使うべきか? {#when-should-you-use-a-liveness-probe}\\n\\n{{< feature-state for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.0\\\" state=\\\"stable\\\" >}}\\n\\nコンテナ自体に問題が発生した場合や状態が悪くなった際にクラッシュすることができればlivenessProbeは不要です。\\nこの場合kubeletが自動でPodの`restartPolicy`に基づいたアクションを実行します。\\n\\nProbeに失敗したときにコンテナを殺したり再起動させたりするには、livenessProbeを設定し`restartPolicy`をAlwaysまたはOnFailureにします。\\n\\n#### readinessProbeをいつ使うべきか? {#when-should-you-use-a-readiness-probe}\\n\\n{{< feature-state for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.0\\\" state=\\\"stable\\\" >}}\\n\\nProbeが成功したときにのみPodにトラフィックを送信したい場合は、readinessProbeを指定します。\\nこの場合readinessProbeはlivenessProbeと同じになる可能性がありますが、readinessProbeが存在するということは、Podがトラフィックを受けずに開始され、Probe成功が開始した後でトラフィックを受け始めることになります。\\n\\nコンテナがメンテナンスのために停止できるようにするには、livenessProbeとは異なる、特定のエンドポイントを確認するreadinessProbeを指定することができます。\\n\\nアプリがバックエンドサービスと厳密な依存関係にある場合、livenessProbeとreadinessProbeの両方を実装することができます。アプリ自体が健全であればlivenessProbeはパスしますが、readinessProbeはさらに、必要なバックエンドサービスが利用可能であるかどうかをチェックします。これにより、エラーメッセージでしか応答できないPodへのトラフィックの転送を避けることができます。\\n\\nコンテナの起動中に大きなデータ、構成ファイル、またはマイグレーションを読み込む必要がある場合は、[startupProbe](#when-should-you-use-a-startup-probe)を使用できます。ただし、失敗したアプリと起動データを処理中のアプリの違いを検出したい場合は、readinessProbeを使用した方が良いかもしれません。\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nPodが削除されたときにリクエストを来ないようにするためには必ずしもreadinessProbeが必要というわけではありません。Podの削除時にはreadinessProbeが存在するかどうかに関係なくPodは自動的に自身をunreadyにします。Pod内のコンテナが停止するのを待つ間Podはunreadyのままです。\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\n#### startupProbeをいつ使うべきか? {#when-should-you-use-a-startup-probe}\\n\\n{{< feature-state for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.20\\\" state=\\\"stable\\\" >}}\\n\\nstartupProbeは、サービスの開始に時間がかかるコンテナを持つPodに役立ちます。livenessProbeの間隔を長く設定するのではなく、コンテナの起動時に別のProbeを構成して、livenessProbeの間隔よりも長い時間を許可できます。\\nコンテナの起動時間が、`initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold x periodSeconds`よりも長い場合は、livenessProbeと同じエンドポイントをチェックするためにstartupProbeを指定します。`periodSeconds`のデフォルトは10秒です。次に、`failureThreshold`をlivenessProbeのデフォルト値を変更せずにコンテナが起動できるように、十分に高い値を設定します。これによりデッドロックを防ぐことができます。\",\n Waiting 상태의 컨테이너는 이미지를 내려받거나(pull), 시크릿을 적용하는 등의 필요한 오퍼레이션이 수행 중인 상태이다. 이 상태와 더불어서, 더 자세한 정보를 제공하기 위해 상태에 대한 메시지와 이유가 출력된다.\n179-\n180-    ```yaml\n181-   ...\n182-      State:          Waiting\n183-       Reason:       ErrImagePull\n184-\t  ...\n185-   ```\n186-\n187-* `Running`: 컨테이너가 이슈 없이 구동된다는 뜻이다. `postStart` 훅(있는 경우)은 컨테이너가 Running 상태가 되기 전에 실행된다. 이 상태는 컨테이너가 언제 Running 상태에 돌입한 시간도 함께 출력된다.\n188-\n189-   ```yaml\n190-   ...\n191-      State:          Running\n192-       Started:      Wed, 30 Jan 2019 16:46:38 +0530\n193-   ...\n194-   ```\n195-\n196-* `Terminated`:  컨테이너가 실행이 완료되어 구동을 멈추었다는 뜻이다. 컨테이너가 성공적으로 작업을 완료했을 때나 어떤 이유에서 실패했을 때 이 상태가 된다. 원인과 종료 코드(exit code)가 컨테이너의 시작과 종료 시간과 함께 무조건 출력된다.\n197-  컨테이너가 Terminated 상태가 되기 전에, `preStop` 훅이 (존재한다면) 실행된다.\n198-\n199-   ```yaml\n200-   ...\n201-      State:          Terminated\n202-        Reason:       Completed\n203-        Exit Code:    0\n204-        Started:      Wed, 30 Jan 2019 11:45:26 +0530\n205-        Finished:     Wed, 30 Jan 2019 11:45:26 +0530\n206-    ...\n207-   ```\n208-\n209-## 파드의 준비성 게이트(readiness gate)\n210-\n211-{{< feature-state for_k8s_version=\"v1.14\" state=\"stable\" >}}\n212-\n213-파드의 준비성에 대한 확장성을 추가하기 위해서\n214-추가적인 피드백이나 신호를 `PodStatus`에 주입하는 방법인,\n215-[파드 준비++](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-network/0007-pod-ready%2B%2B.md)라는 특징이 쿠버네티스 1.11에서 소개되었다.\n216-파드의 준비성을 평가하기 위한 추가적인 조건들을 `PodSpec` 내의 새로운 `ReadinessGate` 필드를\n217-통해서 지정할 수 있다. 만약 쿠버네티스가 `status.conditions` 필드에서 해당하는\n218-조건을 찾지 못한다면, 그 조건의 상태는\n219-기본 값인 \"`False`\"가 된다. 아래는 한 예제를 보여준다.\n220-\n221-```yaml\n222-Kind: Pod\n223-...\n224-spec:","numLines":51,"totalLines":51},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"toolu_01HvSQgaoMKGRRVsKdRjqjXL","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

{#container-probes}\\n\\n*Probe*は[kubelet](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/) により定期的に実行されるコンテナの診断です。診断を行うために、kubeletはコンテナ内でコードを実行するか、ネットワークリクエストします。\\n\\n### チェックのメカニズム {#probe-check-methods}\\n\\nprobeを使ってコンテナをチェックする4つの異なる方法があります。\\n各probeは、この4つの仕組みのうち1つを正確に定義する必要があります:\\n\\n`exec`\\n: コンテナ内で特定のコマンドを実行します。コマンドがステータス0で終了した場合に診断を成功と見なします。\\n\\n`grpc`\\n: [gRPC](https://grpc.io/)を使ってリモートプロシージャコールを実行します。\\n  ターゲットは、[gRPC health checks](https://grpc.io/grpc/core/md_doc_health-checking.html)を実装する必要があります。\\n  レスポンスの`status`が`SERVING`の場合に診断を成功と見なします。\\n  gRPCはアルファ版の機能のため、`GRPCContainerProbe`[フィーチャーゲート](/ja/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/)が\\n  有効の場合のみ利用可能です。\\n\\n`httpGet`\\n: PodのIPアドレスに対して、指定されたポートとパスでHTTP `GET`のリクエストを送信します。\\n  レスポンスのステータスコードが200以上400未満の際に診断を成功とみなします。\\n\\n`tcpSocket`\\n: PodのIPアドレスに対して、指定されたポートでTCPチェックを行います。\\n  そのポートが空いていれば診断を成功とみなします。\\n  オープンしてすぐにリモートシステム(コンテナ)が接続を切断した場合、健全な状態としてカウントします。\\n\\n### Probeの結果 {#probe-outcome}\\n\\n各Probe 次の3つのうちの一つの結果を持ちます:\\n\\n`Success`\\n: コンテナの診断が成功しました。\\n\\n`Failure`\\n: コンテナの診断が失敗しました。\\n\\n`Unknown`\\n: コンテナの診断が失敗しました(何も実行する必要はなく、kubeletはさらにチェックを行います)。\\n\\n### Probeの種類 {#types-of-probe}\\n\\nkubeletは3種類のProbeを実行中のコンテナで行い、また反応することができます:\\n\\n`livenessProbe`\\n: コンテナが動いているかを示します。\\n  livenessProbeに失敗すると、kubeletはコンテナを殺します、そしてコンテナは[restart policy](#restart-policy)に従います。\\n  コンテナにlivenessProbeが設定されていない場合、デフォルトの状態は`Success`です。\\n\\n`readinessProbe`\\n: コンテナがリクエスト応答する準備ができているかを示します。\\n  readinessProbeに失敗すると、エンドポイントコントローラーにより、ServiceからそのPodのIPアドレスが削除されます。\\n  initial delay前のデフォルトのreadinessProbeの初期値は`Failure`です。\\n  コンテナにreadinessProbeが設定されていない場合、デフォルトの状態は`Success`です。\\n\\n`startupProbe`\\n: コンテナ内のアプリケーションが起動したかどうかを示します。\\n  startupProbeが設定された場合、完了するまでその他のすべてのProbeは無効になります。\\n  startupProbeに失敗すると、kubeletはコンテナを殺します、そしてコンテナは[restart policy](#restart-policy)に従います。\\n  コンテナにstartupProbeが設定されていない場合、デフォルトの状態は`Success`です。\\n\\nlivenessProbe、readinessProbeまたはstartupProbeを設定する方法の詳細については、[Liveness Probe、Readiness ProbeおよびStartup Probeを使用する](/ja/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)を参照してください。\\n\\n#### livenessProbeをいつ使うべきか? {#when-should-you-use-a-liveness-probe}\\n\\n{{< feature-state for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.0\\\" state=\\\"stable\\\" >}}\\n\\nコンテナ自体に問題が発生した場合や状態が悪くなった際にクラッシュすることができればlivenessProbeは不要です。\\nこの場合kubeletが自動でPodの`restartPolicy`に基づいたアクションを実行します。\\n\\nProbeに失敗したときにコンテナを殺したり再起動させたりするには、livenessProbeを設定し`restartPolicy`をAlwaysまたはOnFailureにします。\\n\\n#### readinessProbeをいつ使うべきか? {#when-should-you-use-a-readiness-probe}\\n\\n{{< feature-state for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.0\\\" state=\\\"stable\\\" note >}}\\nPodが削除されたときにリクエストを来ないようにするためには必ずしもreadinessProbeが必要というわけではありません。Podの削除時にはreadinessProbeが存在するかどうかに関係なくPodは自動的に自身をunreadyにします。Pod内のコンテナが停止するのを待つ間Podはunreadyのままです。\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\n#### periodSeconds`よりも長い場合は、livenessProbeと同じエンドポイントをチェックするためにstartupProbeを指定します。`periodSeconds`のデフォルトは10秒です。次に、`failureThreshold`をlivenessProbeのデフォルト値を変更せずにコンテナが起動できるように、十分に高い値を設定します。これによりデッドロックを防ぐことができます。\",\n Schemas](/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#specifying-a-structural-schema).\\n\\n#### The messageExpression field\\n\\nSimilar to the `message` field, which defines the string reported for a validation rule failure, \\n`messageExpression` allows you to use a CEL expression to construct the message string.\\nThis allows you to insert more descriptive information into the validation failure message. \\n`messageExpression` must evaluate a string and may use the same variables that are available to the `rule` \\nfield. For example:\\n\\n```yaml\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"self.x <= self.maxLimit\\\"\\n  messageExpression: '\\\"x exceeded max limit of \\\" + string(self.maxLimit)'\\n```\\n\\nKeep in mind that CEL string concatenation (`+` operator) does not auto-cast to string. If\\nyou have a non-string scalar, use the `string(<value>)` function to cast the scalar to a string\\nlike shown in the above example.\\n\\n`messageExpression` must evaluate to a string, and this is checked while the CRD is being written. Note that it is possible\\nto set `message` and `messageExpression` on the same rule, and if both are present, `messageExpression`\\nwill be used. However, if `messageExpression` evaluates to an error, the string defined in `message` \\nwill be used instead, and the `messageExpression` error will be logged. This fallback will also occur if\\nthe CEL expression defined in `messageExpression` generates an empty string, or a string containing line \\nbreaks.\\n\\nIf one of the above conditions are met and no `message` has been set, then the default validation failure\\nmessage will be used instead.\\n\\n`messageExpression` is a CEL expression, so the restrictions listed in [Resource use by validation functions](#resource-use-by-validation-functions) apply. If evaluation halts due to resource constraints \\nduring `messageExpression` execution, then no further validation rules will be executed.\\n\\nSetting `messageExpression` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `message` field {#field-message}\\n\\nIf you want to set a static message, you can supply `message` rather than `messageExpression`.\\nThe value of `message` is used as an opaque error string if validation fails.\\n\\nSetting `message` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `reason` field {#field-reason}\\n\\nYou can add a machine-readable validation failure reason within a `validation`, to be returned\\nwhenever a request fails this validation rule.\\n\\nFor example:\\n\\n```yaml\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"self.x <= self.maxLimit\\\"\\n  reason: \\\"FieldValueInvalid\\\"\\n```\\n\\nThe HTTP status code returned to the caller will match the reason of the first failed validation rule.\\nThe currently supported reasons are: \\\"FieldValueInvalid\\\", \\\"FieldValueForbidden\\\", \\\"FieldValueRequired\\\", \\\"FieldValueDuplicate\\\".\\nIf not set or unknown reasons, default to use \\\"FieldValueInvalid\\\".\\n\\nSetting `reason` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `fieldPath` field {#field-field-path}\\n\\nYou can specify the field path returned when the validation fails.\\n\\nFor example:\\n\\n```yaml\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"self.foo.test.x <= self.maxLimit\\\"\\n  fieldPath: \\\".foo.test.x\\\"\\n```\\n\\nIn the example above, the validation checks the value of field `x` should be less than the value of `maxLimit`.\\nIf no `fieldPath` specified, when validation fails, the fieldPath would be default to wherever `self` scoped.\\nWith `fieldPath` specified, the returned error will have `fieldPath` properly refer to the location of field `x`.\\n\\nThe `fieldPath` value must be a relative JSON path that is scoped to the location of this x-kubernetes-validations extension in the schema. \\nAdditionally, it should refer to an existing field within the schema.\\nFor example when validation checks if a specific attribute `foo` under a map `testMap`, you could set\\n`fieldPath` to `\\\".testMap.foo\\\"` or `.testMap['foo']'`.\\nIf the validation requires checking for unique attributes in two lists, the fieldPath can be set to either of the lists. \\nFor example, it can be set to `.testList1` or `.testList2`.\\nIt supports child operation to refer to an existing field currently. \\nRefer to [JSONPath support in Kubernetes](/docs/reference/kubectl/jsonpath/) for more info.\\nThe `fieldPath` field does not support indexing arrays numerically.\\n\\nSetting `fieldPath` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `optionalOldSelf` field {#field-optional-oldself}\\n\\n{{< feature-state state=\\\"alpha\\\" for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.29\\\" >}}\\n\\nThe feature [CRDValidationRatcheting](#validation-ratcheting) must be enabled in order to \\nmake use of this field.\\n\\nThe `optionalOldSelf` field is a boolean field that alters the behavior of [Transition Rules](#transition-rules) described\\nbelow. Normally, a transition rule will not evaluate if `oldSelf` cannot be determined:\\nduring object creation or when a new value is introduced in an update.\\n\\nIf `optionalOldSelf` is set to true, then transition rules will always be \\nevaluated and the type of `oldSelf` be changed to a CEL [`Optional`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/google/cel-go/cel#OptionalTypes) type. \\n\\n`optionalOldSelf` is useful in cases where schema authors would like a more\\ncontrol tool [than provided by the default equality based behavior of](#validation-ratcheting)\\nto introduce newer, usually stricter constraints on new values, while still \\nallowing old values to be \\\"grandfathered\\\" or ratcheted using the older validation.\\n\\nExample Usage:\\n\\n| CEL                                     | Description |\\n|-----------------------------------------|-------------|\\n| `self.foo == \\\"foo\\\" || (oldSelf.hasValue() && oldSelf.value().foo != \\\"foo\\\")` | Ratcheted rule. Once a value is set to \\\"foo\\\", it must stay foo. But if it existed before the \\\"foo\\\" constraint was introduced, it may use any value |\\n| [oldSelf.orValue(\\\"\\\"), self].all(x, [\\\"OldCase1\\\", \\\"OldCase2\\\"].exists(case, x == case)) || [\\\"NewCase1\\\", \\\"NewCase2\\\"].exists(case, self == case) || [\\\"NewCase\\\"].has(self)` | \\\"Ratcheted validation for removed enum cases if oldSelf used them\\\" |\\n| oldSelf.optMap(o, o.size()).orValue(0) < 4 || self.size() >= 4 | Ratcheted validation of newly increased minimum map or list size |\\n\\n\\n#### Validation functions {#available-validation-functions}\\n\\nFunctions available include:\\n\\n- CEL standard functions, defined in the [list of standard definitions](https://github.com/google/cel-spec/blob/v0.7.0/doc/langdef.md#list-of-standard-definitions)\\n- CEL standard [macros](https://github.com/google/cel-spec/blob/v0.7.0/doc/langdef.md#macros)\\n- CEL [extended string function library](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/google/cel-go@v0.11.2/ext#Strings)\\n- Kubernetes [CEL extension library](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver@v0.24.0/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/library#pkg-functions)\\n\\n#### Transition rules\\n\\nA rule that contains an expression referencing the identifier `oldSelf` is implicitly considered a\\n_transition rule_. Transition rules allow schema authors to prevent certain transitions between two\\notherwise valid states. For example:\\n\\n```yaml\\ntype: string\\nenum: [\\\"low\\\", \\\"medium\\\", \\\"high\\\"]\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"!(self == 'high' && oldSelf == 'low') && !(self == 'low' && oldSelf == 'high')\\\"\\n  message: cannot transition directly between 'low' and 'high'\\n```\\n\\nUnlike other rules, transition rules apply only to operations meeting the following criteria:\\n\\n- The operation updates an existing object. Transition rules never apply to create operations.\\n\\n- Both an old and a new value exist. It remains possible to check if a value has been added or\\n  removed by placing a transition rule on the parent node. Transition rules are never applied to\\n  custom resource creation. When placed on an optional field, a transition rule will not apply to\\n  update operations that set or unset the field.\\n\\n- The path to the schema node being validated by a transition rule must resolve to a node that is\\n  comparable between the old object and the new object. For example, list items and their\\n  descendants (`spec.foo[10].bar`) can't necessarily be correlated between an existing object and a\\n  later update to the same object.\\n\\nErrors will be generated on CRD writes if a schema node contains a transition rule that can never be\\napplied, e.g. \\\"*path*: update rule *rule* cannot be set on schema because the schema or its parent\\nschema is not mergeable\\\".\\n\\nTransition rules are only allowed on _correlatable portions_ of a schema.\\nA portion of the schema is correlatable if all `array` parent schemas are of type `x-kubernetes-list-type=map`;\\nany `set`or `atomic`array parent schemas make it impossible to unambiguously correlate a `self` with `oldSelf`.\\n\\nHere are some examples for transition rules:\\n\\n{{< table caption=\\\"Transition rules examples\\\" >}}\\n| Use Case                                                          | Rule\\n| --------                                                          | --------\\n| Immutability                                                      | `self.foo == oldSelf.foo`\\n| Prevent modification/removal once assigned                        | `oldSelf != 'bar' \\\\|\\\\| self == 'bar'` or `!has(oldSelf.field) \\\\|\\\\| has(self.field)`\\n| Append-only set                                                   | `self.all(element, element in oldSelf)`\\n| If previous value was X, new value can only be A or B, not Y or Z | `oldSelf != 'X' \\\\|\\\\| self in ['A', 'B']`\\n| Monotonic (non-decreasing) counters                               | `self >= oldSelf`\\n{{< /table >}}\\n\\n#### Resource use by validation functions\\n\\nWhen you create or update a CustomResourceDefinition that uses validation rules,\\nthe API server checks the likely impact of running those validation rules. If a rule is\\nestimated to be prohibitively expensive to execute, the API server rejects the create\\nor update operation, and returns an error message.\\nA similar system is used at runtime that observes the actions the interpreter takes. If the interpreter executes\\ntoo many instructions, execution of the rule will be halted, and an error will result.\\nEach CustomResourceDefinition is also allowed a certain amount of resources to finish executing all of\\nits validation rules. If the sum total of its rules are estimated at creation time to go over that limit,\\nthen a validation error will also occur.\\n\\nYou are unlikely to encounter issues with the resource budget for validation if you only\\nspecify rules that always take the same amount of time regardless of how large their input is.\\nFor example, a rule that asserts that `self.foo == 1` does not by itself have any\\nrisk of rejection on validation resource budget groups.\\nBut if `foo` is a string and you define a validation rule `self.foo.contains(\\\"someString\\\")`, that rule takes\\nlonger to execute depending on how long `foo` is.\\nAnother example would be if `foo` were an array, and you specified a validation rule `self.foo.all(x, x > 5)`.\\nThe cost system always assumes the worst-case scenario if a limit on the length of `foo` is not\\ngiven, and this will happen for anything that can be iterated over (lists, maps, etc.).\\n\\nBecause of this, it is considered best practice to put a limit via `maxItems`, `maxProperties`, and\\n`maxLength` for anything that will be processed in a validation rule in order to prevent validation\\nerrors during cost estimation. For example, given this schema with one rule:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      items:\\n        type: string\\n      x-kubernetes-validations:\\n        - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x.contains('a string'))\\\"\\n```\\n\\nthen the API server rejects this rule on validation budget grounds with error:\\n\\n```\\nspec.validation.openAPIV3Schema.properties[spec].properties[foo].x-kubernetes-validations[0].rule: Forbidden:\\nCEL rule exceeded budget by more than 100x (try simplifying the rule, or adding maxItems, maxProperties, and\\nmaxLength where arrays, maps, and strings are used)\\n```\\n\\nThe rejection happens because `self.all` implies calling `contains()` on every string in `foo`,\\nwhich in turn will check the given string to see if it contains `'a string'`. Without limits, this\\nis a very expensive rule.\\n\\nIf you do not specify any validation limit, the estimated cost of this rule will exceed the\\nper-rule cost limit. But if you add limits in the appropriate places, the rule will be allowed:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      maxItems: 25\\n      items:\\n        type: string\\n        maxLength: 10\\n      x-kubernetes-validations:\\n        - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x.contains('a string'))\\\"\\n```\\n\\nThe cost estimation system takes into account how many times the rule will be executed in addition to the\\nestimated cost of the rule itself. For instance, the following rule will have the same estimated cost as the\\nprevious example (despite the rule now being defined on the individual array items):\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      maxItems: 25\\n      items:\\n        type: string\\n        x-kubernetes-validations:\\n          - rule: \\\"self.contains('a string'))\\\"\\n        maxLength: 10\\n```\\n\\nIf a list inside of a list has a validation rule that uses `self.all`, that is significantly more expensive\\nthan a non-nested list with the same rule. A rule that would have been allowed on a non-nested list might need\\nlower limits set on both nested lists in order to be allowed. For example, even without having limits set,\\nthe following rule is allowed:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      items:\\n        type: integer\\n    x-kubernetes-validations:\\n      - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x == 5)\\\"\\n```\\n\\nBut the same rule on the following schema (with a nested array added) produces a validation error:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      items:\\n        type: array\\n        items:\\n          type: integer\\n        x-kubernetes-validations:\\n          - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x == 5)\\\"\\n```\\n\\nThis is because each item of `foo` is itself an array, and each subarray in turn calls `self.all`.\\nAvoid nested lists and maps if possible where validation rules are used.\",\n7\t \"oracle_target\": \"```yaml\\napiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1\\nkind: CustomResourceDefinition\\nmetadata:\\n  name: crontabs.stable.example.com\\nspec:\\n  group: stable.example.com\\n  versions:\\n    - Schemas](/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definitions/#specifying-a-structural-schema).\\n\\n#### The messageExpression field\\n\\nSimilar to the `message` field, which defines the string reported for a validation rule failure, \\n`messageExpression` allows you to use a CEL expression to construct the message string.\\nThis allows you to insert more descriptive information into the validation failure message. \\n`messageExpression` must evaluate a string and may use the same variables that are available to the `rule` \\nfield. For example:\\n\\n```yaml\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"self.x <= self.maxLimit\\\"\\n  messageExpression: '\\\"x exceeded max limit of \\\" + string(self.maxLimit)'\\n```\\n\\nKeep in mind that CEL string concatenation (`+` operator) does not auto-cast to string. If\\nyou have a non-string scalar, use the `string(<value>)` function to cast the scalar to a string\\nlike shown in the above example.\\n\\n`messageExpression` must evaluate to a string, and this is checked while the CRD is being written. Note that it is possible\\nto set `message` and `messageExpression` on the same rule, and if both are present, `messageExpression`\\nwill be used. However, if `messageExpression` evaluates to an error, the string defined in `message` \\nwill be used instead, and the `messageExpression` error will be logged. This fallback will also occur if\\nthe CEL expression defined in `messageExpression` generates an empty string, or a string containing line \\nbreaks.\\n\\nIf one of the above conditions are met and no `message` has been set, then the default validation failure\\nmessage will be used instead.\\n\\n`messageExpression` is a CEL expression, so the restrictions listed in [Resource use by validation functions](#resource-use-by-validation-functions) apply. If evaluation halts due to resource constraints \\nduring `messageExpression` execution, then no further validation rules will be executed.\\n\\nSetting `messageExpression` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `message` field {#field-message}\\n\\nIf you want to set a static message, you can supply `message` rather than `messageExpression`.\\nThe value of `message` is used as an opaque error string if validation fails.\\n\\nSetting `message` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `reason` field {#field-reason}\\n\\nYou can add a machine-readable validation failure reason within a `validation`, to be returned\\nwhenever a request fails this validation rule.\\n\\nFor example:\\n\\n```yaml\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"self.x <= self.maxLimit\\\"\\n  reason: \\\"FieldValueInvalid\\\"\\n```\\n\\nThe HTTP status code returned to the caller will match the reason of the first failed validation rule.\\nThe currently supported reasons are: \\\"FieldValueInvalid\\\", \\\"FieldValueForbidden\\\", \\\"FieldValueRequired\\\", \\\"FieldValueDuplicate\\\".\\nIf not set or unknown reasons, default to use \\\"FieldValueInvalid\\\".\\n\\nSetting `reason` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `fieldPath` field {#field-field-path}\\n\\nYou can specify the field path returned when the validation fails.\\n\\nFor example:\\n\\n```yaml\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"self.foo.test.x <= self.maxLimit\\\"\\n  fieldPath: \\\".foo.test.x\\\"\\n```\\n\\nIn the example above, the validation checks the value of field `x` should be less than the value of `maxLimit`.\\nIf no `fieldPath` specified, when validation fails, the fieldPath would be default to wherever `self` scoped.\\nWith `fieldPath` specified, the returned error will have `fieldPath` properly refer to the location of field `x`.\\n\\nThe `fieldPath` value must be a relative JSON path that is scoped to the location of this x-kubernetes-validations extension in the schema. \\nAdditionally, it should refer to an existing field within the schema.\\nFor example when validation checks if a specific attribute `foo` under a map `testMap`, you could set\\n`fieldPath` to `\\\".testMap.foo\\\"` or `.testMap['foo']'`.\\nIf the validation requires checking for unique attributes in two lists, the fieldPath can be set to either of the lists. \\nFor example, it can be set to `.testList1` or `.testList2`.\\nIt supports child operation to refer to an existing field currently. \\nRefer to [JSONPath support in Kubernetes](/docs/reference/kubectl/jsonpath/) for more info.\\nThe `fieldPath` field does not support indexing arrays numerically.\\n\\nSetting `fieldPath` is optional.\\n\\n#### The `optionalOldSelf` field {#field-optional-oldself}\\n\\n{{< feature-state state=\\\"alpha\\\" for_k8s_version=\\\"v1.29\\\" >}}\\n\\nThe feature [CRDValidationRatcheting](#validation-ratcheting) must be enabled in order to \\nmake use of this field.\\n\\nThe `optionalOldSelf` field is a boolean field that alters the behavior of [Transition Rules](#transition-rules) described\\nbelow. Normally, a transition rule will not evaluate if `oldSelf` cannot be determined:\\nduring object creation or when a new value is introduced in an update.\\n\\nIf `optionalOldSelf` is set to true, then transition rules will always be \\nevaluated and the type of `oldSelf` be changed to a CEL [`Optional`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/google/cel-go/cel#OptionalTypes) type. \\n\\n`optionalOldSelf` is useful in cases where schema authors would like a more\\ncontrol tool [than provided by the default equality based behavior of](#validation-ratcheting)\\nto introduce newer, usually stricter constraints on new values, while still \\nallowing old values to be \\\"grandfathered\\\" or ratcheted using the older validation.\\n\\nExample Usage:\\n\\n| CEL                                     | Description |\\n|-----------------------------------------|-------------|\\n| `self.foo == \\\"foo\\\" || (oldSelf.hasValue() && oldSelf.value().foo != \\\"foo\\\")` | Ratcheted rule. Once a value is set to \\\"foo\\\", it must stay foo. But if it existed before the \\\"foo\\\" constraint was introduced, it may use any value |\\n| [oldSelf.orValue(\\\"\\\"), self].all(x, [\\\"OldCase1\\\", \\\"OldCase2\\\"].exists(case, x == case)) || [\\\"NewCase1\\\", \\\"NewCase2\\\"].exists(case, self == case) || [\\\"NewCase\\\"].has(self)` | \\\"Ratcheted validation for removed enum cases if oldSelf used them\\\" |\\n| oldSelf.optMap(o, o.size()).orValue(0) < 4 || self.size() >= 4 | Ratcheted validation of newly increased minimum map or list size |\\n\\n\\n#### Validation functions {#available-validation-functions}\\n\\nFunctions available include:\\n\\n- CEL standard functions, defined in the [list of standard definitions](https://github.com/google/cel-spec/blob/v0.7.0/doc/langdef.md#list-of-standard-definitions)\\n- CEL standard [macros](https://github.com/google/cel-spec/blob/v0.7.0/doc/langdef.md#macros)\\n- CEL [extended string function library](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/google/cel-go@v0.11.2/ext#Strings)\\n- Kubernetes [CEL extension library](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver@v0.24.0/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/library#pkg-functions)\\n\\n#### Transition rules\\n\\nA rule that contains an expression referencing the identifier `oldSelf` is implicitly considered a\\n_transition rule_. Transition rules allow schema authors to prevent certain transitions between two\\notherwise valid states. For example:\\n\\n```yaml\\ntype: string\\nenum: [\\\"low\\\", \\\"medium\\\", \\\"high\\\"]\\nx-kubernetes-validations:\\n- rule: \\\"!(self == 'high' && oldSelf == 'low') && !(self == 'low' && oldSelf == 'high')\\\"\\n  message: cannot transition directly between 'low' and 'high'\\n```\\n\\nUnlike other rules, transition rules apply only to operations meeting the following criteria:\\n\\n- The operation updates an existing object. Transition rules never apply to create operations.\\n\\n- Both an old and a new value exist. It remains possible to check if a value has been added or\\n  removed by placing a transition rule on the parent node. Transition rules are never applied to\\n  custom resource creation. When placed on an optional field, a transition rule will not apply to\\n  update operations that set or unset the field.\\n\\n- The path to the schema node being validated by a transition rule must resolve to a node that is\\n  comparable between the old object and the new object. For example, list items and their\\n  descendants (`spec.foo[10].bar`) can't necessarily be correlated between an existing object and a\\n  later update to the same object.\\n\\nErrors will be generated on CRD writes if a schema node contains a transition rule that can never be\\napplied, e.g. \\\"*path*: update rule *rule* cannot be set on schema because the schema or its parent\\nschema is not mergeable\\\".\\n\\nTransition rules are only allowed on _correlatable portions_ of a schema.\\nA portion of the schema is correlatable if all `array` parent schemas are of type `x-kubernetes-list-type=map`;\\nany `set`or `atomic`array parent schemas make it impossible to unambiguously correlate a `self` with `oldSelf`.\\n\\nHere are some examples for transition rules:\\n\\n{{< table caption=\\\"Transition rules examples\\\" >}}\\n| Use Case                                                          | Rule\\n| --------                                                          | --------\\n| Immutability                                                      | `self.foo == oldSelf.foo`\\n| Prevent modification/removal once assigned                        | `oldSelf != 'bar' \\\\|\\\\| self == 'bar'` or `!has(oldSelf.field) \\\\|\\\\| has(self.field)`\\n| Append-only set                                                   | `self.all(element, element in oldSelf)`\\n| If previous value was X, new value can only be A or B, not Y or Z | `oldSelf != 'X' \\\\|\\\\| self in ['A', 'B']`\\n| Monotonic (non-decreasing) counters                               | `self >= oldSelf`\\n{{< /table >}}\\n\\n#### Resource use by validation functions\\n\\nWhen you create or update a CustomResourceDefinition that uses validation rules,\\nthe API server checks the likely impact of running those validation rules. If a rule is\\nestimated to be prohibitively expensive to execute, the API server rejects the create\\nor update operation, and returns an error message.\\nA similar system is used at runtime that observes the actions the interpreter takes. If the interpreter executes\\ntoo many instructions, execution of the rule will be halted, and an error will result.\\nEach CustomResourceDefinition is also allowed a certain amount of resources to finish executing all of\\nits validation rules. If the sum total of its rules are estimated at creation time to go over that limit,\\nthen a validation error will also occur.\\n\\nYou are unlikely to encounter issues with the resource budget for validation if you only\\nspecify rules that always take the same amount of time regardless of how large their input is.\\nFor example, a rule that asserts that `self.foo == 1` does not by itself have any\\nrisk of rejection on validation resource budget groups.\\nBut if `foo` is a string and you define a validation rule `self.foo.contains(\\\"someString\\\")`, that rule takes\\nlonger to execute depending on how long `foo` is.\\nAnother example would be if `foo` were an array, and you specified a validation rule `self.foo.all(x, x > 5)`.\\nThe cost system always assumes the worst-case scenario if a limit on the length of `foo` is not\\ngiven, and this will happen for anything that can be iterated over (lists, maps, etc.).\\n\\nBecause of this, it is considered best practice to put a limit via `maxItems`, `maxProperties`, and\\n`maxLength` for anything that will be processed in a validation rule in order to prevent validation\\nerrors during cost estimation. For example, given this schema with one rule:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      items:\\n        type: string\\n      x-kubernetes-validations:\\n        - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x.contains('a string'))\\\"\\n```\\n\\nthen the API server rejects this rule on validation budget grounds with error:\\n\\n```\\nspec.validation.openAPIV3Schema.properties[spec].properties[foo].x-kubernetes-validations[0].rule: Forbidden:\\nCEL rule exceeded budget by more than 100x (try simplifying the rule, or adding maxItems, maxProperties, and\\nmaxLength where arrays, maps, and strings are used)\\n```\\n\\nThe rejection happens because `self.all` implies calling `contains()` on every string in `foo`,\\nwhich in turn will check the given string to see if it contains `'a string'`. Without limits, this\\nis a very expensive rule.\\n\\nIf you do not specify any validation limit, the estimated cost of this rule will exceed the\\nper-rule cost limit. But if you add limits in the appropriate places, the rule will be allowed:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      maxItems: 25\\n      items:\\n        type: string\\n        maxLength: 10\\n      x-kubernetes-validations:\\n        - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x.contains('a string'))\\\"\\n```\\n\\nThe cost estimation system takes into account how many times the rule will be executed in addition to the\\nestimated cost of the rule itself. For instance, the following rule will have the same estimated cost as the\\nprevious example (despite the rule now being defined on the individual array items):\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      maxItems: 25\\n      items:\\n        type: string\\n        x-kubernetes-validations:\\n          - rule: \\\"self.contains('a string'))\\\"\\n        maxLength: 10\\n```\\n\\nIf a list inside of a list has a validation rule that uses `self.all`, that is significantly more expensive\\nthan a non-nested list with the same rule. A rule that would have been allowed on a non-nested list might need\\nlower limits set on both nested lists in order to be allowed. For example, even without having limits set,\\nthe following rule is allowed:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      items:\\n        type: integer\\n    x-kubernetes-validations:\\n      - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x == 5)\\\"\\n```\\n\\nBut the same rule on the following schema (with a nested array added) produces a validation error:\\n\\n```yaml\\nopenAPIV3Schema:\\n  type: object\\n  properties:\\n    foo:\\n      type: array\\n      items:\\n        type: array\\n        items:\\n          type: integer\\n        x-kubernetes-validations:\\n          - rule: \\\"self.all(x, x == 5)\\\"\\n```\\n\\nThis is because each item of `foo` is itself an array, and each subarray in turn calls `self.all`.\\nAvoid nested lists and maps if possible where validation rules are used.\",\n \"oracle_target\": \"```yaml\\napiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1\\nkind: CustomResourceDefinition\\nmetadata:\\n  name: crontabs.stable.example.com\\nspec:\\n  group: stable.example.com\\n  versions:\\n    - Such information might otherwise be put in a\\nPod specification or in an image. Users can create secrets and the system\\nalso creates some secrets.\\n\\nTo use a secret, a Pod needs to reference the secret.\\nA secret can be used with a Pod in two ways:\\n\\n- As files in a\\n{{< glossary_tooltip text=\\\"volume\\\" term_id=\\\"volume\\\" >}} mounted on one or more of\\nits containers.\\n- By the kubelet when pulling images for the Pod.\\n\\n### Built-in Secrets\\n\\n#### Service accounts automatically create and attach Secrets with API credentials\\n\\nKubernetes automatically creates secrets which contain credentials for\\naccessing the API and automatically modifies your Pods to use this type of\\nsecret.\\n\\nThe automatic creation and use of API credentials can be disabled or overridden\\nif desired.  However, if all you need to do is securely access the API server,\\nthis is the recommended workflow.\\n\\nSee the [ServiceAccount](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/)\\ndocumentation for more information on how service accounts work.\\n\\n### Creating your own Secrets\\n\\n#### Creating a Secret Using `kubectl`\\n\\nSecrets can contain user credentials required by Pods to access a database.\\nFor example, a database connection string\\nconsists of a username and password. You can store the username in a file `./username.txt`\\nand the password in a file `./password.txt` on your local machine.\\n\\n```shell\\n# Create files needed for the rest of the example.\\necho -n 'admin' > ./username.txt\\necho -n '1f2d1e2e67df' > ./password.txt\\n```\\n\\nThe `kubectl create secret` command packages these files into a Secret and creates\\nthe object on the API server.\\nThe name of a Secret object must be a valid\\n[DNS subdomain name](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names#dns-subdomain-names).\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl create secret generic db-user-pass --from-file=./username.txt --from-file=./password.txt\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```\\nsecret \\\"db-user-pass\\\" created\\n```\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nSpecial characters such as `$`, `\\\\`, `*`, and `!` will be interpreted by your [shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_(computing)) and require escaping.\\nIn most shells, the easiest way to escape the password is to surround it with single quotes (`'`).\\nFor example, if your actual password is `S!B\\\\*d$zDsb`, you should execute the command this way:\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl create secret generic dev-db-secret --from-literal=username=devuser --from-literal=password='S!B\\\\*d$zDsb'\\n```\\n\\nYou do not need to escape special characters in passwords from files (`--from-file`).\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\nYou can check that the secret was created:\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl get secrets\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```\\nNAME                  TYPE                                  DATA      AGE\\ndb-user-pass          Opaque                                2         51s\\n```\\n\\nYou can view a description of the secret:\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl describe secrets/db-user-pass\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```\\nName:            db-user-pass\\nNamespace:       default\\nLabels:          <none>\\nAnnotations:     <none>\\n\\nType:            Opaque\\n\\nData\\n====\\npassword.txt:    12 bytes\\nusername.txt:    5 bytes\\n```\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nThe commands `kubectl get` and `kubectl describe` avoid showing the contents of a secret by\\ndefault. This is to protect the secret from being exposed accidentally to an onlooker,\\nor from being stored in a terminal log.\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\nSee [decoding a secret](#decoding-a-secret) to learn how to view the contents of a secret.\\n\\n#### Creating a Secret manually\\n\\nYou can also create a Secret in a file first, in JSON or YAML format,\\nand then create that object.\\nThe name of a Secret object must be a valid\\n[DNS subdomain name](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names#dns-subdomain-names).\\nThe [Secret](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param \\\"version\\\" >}}/#secret-v1-core)\\ncontains two maps:\\n`data` and `stringData`. The `data` field is used to store arbitrary data, encoded using\\nbase64. The `stringData` field is provided for convenience, and allows you to provide\\nsecret data as unencoded strings.\\n\\nFor example, to store two strings in a Secret using the `data` field, convert\\nthe strings to base64 as follows:\\n\\n```shell\\necho -n 'admin' | base64\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```\\nYWRtaW4=\\n```\\n\\n```shell\\necho -n '1f2d1e2e67df' | base64\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```\\nMWYyZDFlMmU2N2Rm\\n```\\n\\nWrite a Secret that looks like this:\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: Secret\\nmetadata:\\n  name: mysecret\\ntype: Opaque\\ndata:\\n  username: YWRtaW4=\\n  password: MWYyZDFlMmU2N2Rm\\n```\\n\\nNow create the Secret using [`kubectl apply`](/docs/reference/generated/kubectl/kubectl-commands#apply):\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl apply -f ./secret.yaml\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```\\nsecret \\\"mysecret\\\" created\\n```\\n\\nFor certain scenarios, you may wish to use the `stringData` field instead. This\\nfield allows you to put a non-base64 encoded string directly into the Secret,\\nand the string will be encoded for you when the Secret is created or updated.\\n\\nA practical example of this might be where you are deploying an application\\nthat uses a Secret to store a configuration file, and you want to populate\\nparts of that configuration file during your deployment process.\\n\\nFor example, if your application uses the following configuration file:\\n\\n```yaml\\napiUrl: \\\"https://my.api.com/api/v1\\\"\\nusername: \\\"user\\\"\\npassword: \\\"password\\\"\\n```\\n\\nYou could store this in a Secret using the following definition:\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: Secret\\nmetadata:\\n  name: mysecret\\ntype: Opaque\\nstringData:\\n  config.yaml: |-\\n    apiUrl: \\\"https://my.api.com/api/v1\\\"\\n    username: {{username}}\\n    password: {{password}}\\n```\\n\\nYour deployment tool could then replace the `{{username}}` and `{{password}}`\\ntemplate variables before running `kubectl apply`.\\n\\nThe `stringData` field is a write-only convenience field. It is never output when\\nretrieving Secrets. For example, if you run the following command:\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl get secret mysecret -o yaml\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: Secret\\nmetadata:\\n  creationTimestamp: 2018-11-15T20:40:59Z\\n  name: mysecret\\n  namespace: default\\n  resourceVersion: \\\"7225\\\"\\n  uid: c280ad2e-e916-11e8-98f2-025000000001\\ntype: Opaque\\ndata:\\n  config.yaml: YXBpVXJsOiAiaHR0cHM6Ly9teS5hcGkuY29tL2FwaS92MSIKdXNlcm5hbWU6IHt7dXNlcm5hbWV9fQpwYXNzd29yZDoge3twYXNzd29yZH19\\n```\\n\\nIf a field, such as `username`, is specified in both `data` and `stringData`,\\nthe value from `stringData` is used. For example, the following Secret definition:\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: Secret\\nmetadata:\\n  name: mysecret\\ntype: Opaque\\ndata:\\n  username: YWRtaW4=\\nstringData:\\n  username: administrator\\n```\\n\\nResults in the following Secret:\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: Secret\\nmetadata:\\n  creationTimestamp: 2018-11-15T20:46:46Z\\n  name: mysecret\\n  namespace: default\\n  resourceVersion: \\\"7579\\\"\\n  uid: 91460ecb-e917-11e8-98f2-025000000001\\ntype: Opaque\\ndata:\\n  username: YWRtaW5pc3RyYXRvcg==\\n```\\n\\nWhere `YWRtaW5pc3RyYXRvcg==` decodes to `administrator`.\\n\\nThe keys of `data` and `stringData` must consist of alphanumeric characters,\\n'-', '_' or '.'.\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nThe serialized JSON and YAML values of secret data are\\nencoded as base64 strings. Newlines are not valid within these strings and must\\nbe omitted. When using the `base64` utility on Darwin/macOS, users should avoid\\nusing the `-b` option to split long lines. The `data` and the `stringData` fields are optional.\\nThe values for all keys in the `data` field have to be base64-encoded strings.\\nIf the conversion to base64 string is not desirable, you can choose to specify\\nthe `stringData` field instead, which accepts arbitrary strings as values.\\n\\nThe keys of `data` and `stringData` must consist of alphanumeric characters,\\n`-`, `_` or `.`. All key-value pairs in the `stringData` field are internally\\nmerged into the `data` field. If a key appears in both the `data` and the\\n`stringData` field, the value specified in the `stringData` field takes\\nprecedence.\\n\\n#### Size limit {#restriction-data-size}\\n\\nIndividual secrets are limited to 1MiB in size. This is to discourage creation\\nof very large secrets that could exhaust the API server and kubelet memory.\\nHowever, creation of many smaller secrets could also exhaust memory. You can\\nuse a [resource quota](/docs/concepts/policy/resource-quotas/) to limit the\\nnumber of Secrets (or other resources) in a namespace.\\n\\n### Editing a Secret\\n\\nYou can edit an existing Secret unless it is [immutable](#secret-immutable). To\\nedit a Secret, use one of the following methods:\\n\\n- [Use `kubectl`](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kubectl/#edit-secret)\\n- [Use a configuration file](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-config-file/#edit-secret)\\n\\nYou can also edit the data in a Secret using the [Kustomize tool](/docs/tasks/configmap-secret/managing-secret-using-kustomize/#edit-secret). However, this\\nmethod creates a new `Secret` object with the edited data.\\n\\nDepending on how you created the Secret, as well as how the Secret is used in\\nyour Pods, updates to existing `Secret` objects are propagated automatically to\\nPods that use the data. For more information, refer to [Using Secrets as files from a Pod](#using-secrets-as-files-from-a-pod) section.\\n\\n### Using a Secret\\n\\nSecrets can be mounted as data volumes or exposed as\\n{{< glossary_tooltip text=\\\"environment variables\\\" term_id=\\\"container-env-variables\\\" >}}\\nto be used by a container in a Pod. Secrets can also be used by other parts of the\\nsystem, without being directly exposed to the Pod. For example, Secrets can hold\\ncredentials that other parts of the system should use to interact with external\\nsystems on your behalf.\\n\\nSecret volume sources are validated to ensure that the specified object\\nreference actually points to an object of type Secret. Therefore, a Secret\\nneeds to be created before any Pods that depend on it.\\n\\nIf the Secret cannot be fetched (perhaps because it does not exist, or\\ndue to a temporary lack of connection to the API server) the kubelet\\nperiodically retries running that Pod. The kubelet also reports an Event\\nfor that Pod, including details of the problem fetching the Secret.\\n\\n#### Optional Secrets {#restriction-secret-must-exist}\\n\\nWhen you reference a Secret in a Pod, you can mark the Secret as _optional_,\\nsuch as in the following example. If an optional Secret doesn't exist,\\nKubernetes ignores it.\\n\\n```yaml\\napiVersion: v1\\nkind: Pod\\nmetadata:\\n  name: mypod\\nspec:\\n  containers:\\n  - name: mypod\\n    image: redis\\n    volumeMounts:\\n    - name: foo\\n      mountPath: \\\"/etc/foo\\\"\\n      readOnly: true\\n  volumes:\\n  - name: foo\\n    secret:\\n      secretName: mysecret\\n      optional: true\\n```\\n\\nBy default, Secrets are required. None of a Pod's containers will start until\\nall non-optional Secrets are available.\\n\\nIf a Pod references a specific key in a non-optional Secret and that Secret\\ndoes exist, but is missing the named key, the Pod fails during startup.\\n\\n### Using Secrets as files from a Pod {#using-secrets-as-files-from-a-pod}\\n\\nIf you want to access data from a Secret in a Pod, one way to do that is to\\nhave Kubernetes make the value of that Secret be available as a file inside\\nthe filesystem of one or more of the Pod's containers.\\n\\nFor instructions, refer to\\n[Distribute credentials securely using Secrets](/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/distribute-credentials-secure/#create-a-pod-that-has-access-to-the-secret-data-through-a-volume).\\n\\nWhen a volume contains data from a Secret, and that Secret is updated, Kubernetes tracks\\nthis and updates the data in the volume, using an eventually-consistent approach.\\n\\n{{< note >}}\\nA container using a Secret as a\\n[subPath](/docs/concepts/storage/volumes#using-subpath) volume mount does not receive\\nautomated Secret updates.\\n{{< /note >}}\\n\\nThe kubelet keeps a cache of the current keys and values for the Secrets that are used in\\nvolumes for pods on that node.\\nYou can configure the way that the kubelet detects changes from the cached values. The\\n`configMapAndSecretChangeDetectionStrategy` field in the\\n[kubelet configuration](/docs/reference/config-api/kubelet-config.v1beta1/) controls\\nwhich strategy the kubelet uses. The default strategy is `Watch`.\\n\\nUpdates to Secrets can be either propagated by an API watch mechanism (the default), based on\\na cache with a defined time-to-live, or polled from the cluster API server on each kubelet\\nsynchronisation loop.\\n\\nAs a result, the total delay from the moment when the Secret is updated to the moment\\nwhen new keys are projected to the Pod can be as long as the kubelet sync period + cache\\npropagation delay, where the cache propagation delay depends on the chosen cache type\\n(following the same order listed in the previous paragraph, these are:\\nwatch propagation delay, the configured cache TTL, or zero for direct polling).\\n\\n### Using Secrets as environment variables\\n\\nTo use a Secret in an {{< glossary_tooltip text=\\\"environment variable\\\" term_id=\\\"container-env-variables\\\" >}}\\nin a Pod:\\n\\n1. For each container in your Pod specification, add an environment variable\\n   for each Secret key that you want to use to the\\n   `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef` field.\\n1. Modify your image and/or command line so that the program looks for values\\n   in the specified environment variables.\\n\\nFor instructions, refer to\\n[Define container environment variables using Secret data](/docs/tasks/inject-data-application/distribute-credentials-secure/#define-container-environment-variables-using-secret-data).\\n\\n#### Invalid environment variables {#restriction-env-from-invalid}\\n\\nIf your environment variable definitions in your Pod specification are\\nconsidered to be invalid environment variable names, those keys aren't made\\navailable to your container. The Pod is allowed to start.\\n\\nKubernetes adds an Event with the reason set to `InvalidVariableNames` and a\\nmessage that lists the skipped invalid keys. The following example shows a Pod that refers to a Secret named `mysecret`, where `mysecret` contains 2 invalid keys: `1badkey` and `2alsobad`.\\n\\n```shell\\nkubectl get events\\n```\\n\\nThe output is similar to:\\n\\n```\\nLASTSEEN   FIRSTSEEN   COUNT     NAME            KIND      SUBOBJECT                         TYPE      REASON\\n0s         0s          1         dapi-test-pod   Pod                                         Warning   InvalidEnvironmentVariableNames   kubelet, 127.0.0.1      Keys [1badkey, 2alsobad] from the EnvFrom secret default/mysecret were skipped since they are considered invalid environment variable names.\\n```\\n\\n### Container image pull secrets {#using-imagepullsecrets}\\n\\nIf you want to fetch container images from a private repository, you need a way for\\nthe kubelet on each node to authenticate to that repository. You can configure\\n_image pull secrets_ to make this possible. rules fail.\\nCompilation process includes type checking as well.\\n\\nThe compilation failure:\\n\\n- `no_matching_overload`: this function has no overload for the types of the arguments.\\n\\n  For This includes:\\n\\n- Unknown field values that are preserved by object schemas with `x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields`.\\n- Object properties where the property schema is of an \\\"unknown type\\\". Concatenation on arrays with x-kubernetes-list-type use the semantics of\\nthe list type:\\n\\n- `set`: `X + Y` performs a union where the array positions of all elements in `X` are preserved\\n  and non-intersecting elements in `Y` are appended, retaining their partial order.\\n\\n- `map`: `X + Y` performs a merge where the array positions of all keys in `X` are preserved but\\n  the values are overwritten by values in `Y` when the key sets of `X` and `Y` intersect.
